sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A developer asks you which kind of shared access signature (SAS) can be created without the application ever holding a storage account access key. Which SAS type is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key?
opzione_d: Service SAS that references a stored access policy
spiegazione: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key that is obtained from Microsoft Entra ID by calling Get User Delegation Key, so the application never needs the storage account key. Microsoft recommends this type for superior security. Account SAS is wrong because it is signed with the storage account key (Shared Key). Service SAS is wrong for the same reason: it is also signed with the account key. A service SAS that references a stored access policy is still a service SAS and is still signed with the account key; the stored access policy only adds server-side control over the constraints, it does not change the signing credential.
tags: sas,user delegation sas,microsoft entra id,storage,shared key

domanda: While planning delegated access to a blob container, you decide to group your service SAS tokens under stored access policies. What is the maximum number of stored access policies that you can set on a single container at one time?
spiegazione: You can set a maximum of five access policies on a container, table, queue, or share at one time; each SignedIdentifier element with its unique Id corresponds to one policy. Attempting to set more than five at once causes the service to return status code 400 (Bad Request). 1 is wrong: multiple policies per container are explicitly supported. 10 and 50 are wrong: they are plausible-looking but incorrect limits; the documented limit is five per resource.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A contractor accidentally posted an ad hoc service SAS URI for a blob in a public ticketing system. The SAS was signed with key1, does not reference any stored access policy, and is valid for another 20 days. You must invalidate the token immediately. What should you do?
opzione_a: Regenerate the storage account access key that was used to sign the SAS.
opzione_b: Create a stored access policy on the container with an expiry time in the past.
opzione_c: Set the public access level of the container to Private (no anonymous access).
opzione_d: Configure a SAS expiration policy on the storage account and set the expiration action to Log.
spiegazione: Regenerating the account key that was used to create the signature is the only way to immediately revoke an ad hoc SAS, because the signature is validated against that key. Creating a stored access policy afterwards has no effect: the already-issued token does not carry a signedIdentifier (si) value, so it is not bound to any policy. Changing the container public access level only controls anonymous access; a SAS is authorized by its signature and continues to work. A SAS expiration policy with the Log action only warns the creator and writes a SasExpiryStatus entry to the logs when an out-of-policy SAS is used; it does not block or revoke tokens that were already issued.

domanda: Your security team requires that any delegated access token issued for a blob container can be revoked at any time without regenerating the storage account access keys, because dozens of internal applications depend on those keys. Which approach meets the requirement?
opzione_a: Issue an account SAS and reduce the expiry time to one hour.
opzione_b: Issue a service SAS that references a stored access policy defined on the container.
opzione_c: Issue an ad hoc service SAS and rely on a near-term expiry time.
opzione_d: Enable a SAS expiration policy on the storage account with the Block action.
spiegazione: Stored access policies give you the option to revoke permissions for a service SAS without having to regenerate the storage account keys: you can delete the policy, change its signed identifier, or move its expiry time into the past, and the change immediately affects every SAS associated with it. An account SAS cannot reference a stored access policy (stored access policies are not supported for account SAS or user delegation SAS), so a short expiry is the only control and it does not provide revocation. An ad hoc service SAS with a near-term expiry is a good mitigation but still cannot be revoked without regenerating the key. A SAS expiration policy with Block enforces an upper limit on the validity interval for newly created signatures; it is not a per-token revocation mechanism and would not selectively revoke one partner's token.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: An application requests a user delegation key by calling the Get User Delegation Key operation and then uses that key to sign multiple user delegation SAS tokens. What is the maximum period for which the user delegation key can be valid?
spiegazione: You can specify that a user delegation key is valid for a period of up to seven days. The signedKeyExpiryTime (ske) value may be a maximum of seven days from the start time of the SAS, and a user delegation SAS therefore has a maximum expiry interval of 7 days regardless of any SAS expiration policy. 1 hour is wrong: it is the legacy limit for a service SAS that used a REST version prior to 2012-02-12 and did not reference a stored access policy. 24 hours and 90 days are wrong: they are not documented limits for the user delegation key.
tags: user delegation sas,user delegation key,expiry,seven days

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A monitoring tool must be able to call List Containers, read and set Blob service properties, create and delete containers, and also read messages from queues in the same storage account. You must delegate this access with a single signature and without granting the tool an account key permanently. Which type of SAS must you generate?
opzione_a: A service SAS scoped to a container (sr=c)
opzione_c: A user delegation SAS scoped to the container
opzione_d: A service SAS that references a stored access policy
spiegazione: Only an account SAS can delegate access to service-level operations such as Get/Set Service Properties, Get Service Stats, and List Containers, and only an account SAS can span more than one storage service (for example Blob and Queue) in a single signature. It also permits create and delete operations on containers and queues. A service SAS scoped to a container is wrong: a service SAS delegates access to a resource in only one service and explicitly cannot create, delete, or list containers, nor read or write container metadata and properties. A user delegation SAS scoped to a container is wrong: it is scoped to a single service resource and cannot cover both blob service-level operations and queue messages with one token. A service SAS that references a stored access policy is still a service SAS and inherits the same restrictions on service-level and container-management operations.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A service principal named app1 is assigned the Storage Blob Data Reader role, scoped to a single blob container in storage account sa1. When app1 calls Get User Delegation Key, the call fails. You must allow app1 to create user delegation SAS tokens while granting the fewest additional permissions. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign the Storage Blob Delegator role to app1 at the scope of the storage account.
opzione_b: Assign the Storage Account Contributor role to app1 at the scope of the storage account.
opzione_c: Assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role to app1 at the scope of the subscription.
opzione_d: Assign the Reader role to app1 at the scope of the resource group.
spiegazione: The Get User Delegation Key operation acts at the level of the storage account, so the generateUserDelegationKey action must be granted at the storage account, resource group, or subscription scope. When a principal already has a data-access role scoped to a container, Microsoft's documented guidance is to additionally assign a delegator role such as Storage Blob Delegator at the account, resource group, or subscription scope. Storage Account Contributor also includes the action but grants broad management permissions over the account, including access to the account keys, so it violates least privilege. Re-assigning Storage Blob Data Reader at subscription scope would work technically but grants read access to blob data across every storage account in the subscription, which is far more than required. The Reader role grants no data actions and does not include the generateUserDelegationKey action, so the call would still fail.
tags: user delegation sas,storage blob delegator,rbac,scope,least privilege

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Litware runs Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts that are Microsoft Entra joined and have no network connectivity to the company's on-premises domain controllers. User accounts originate in on-premises AD DS and are synced to Microsoft Entra ID with Microsoft Entra Connect Sync. You must let these users authenticate to an SMB Azure file share by using their existing credentials. Which identity source should you enable on the storage account?
opzione_a: On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)
opzione_d: Shared Key authorization with the storage account key
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra ID issue the Kerberos tickets used to reach the share over SMB, so end users can access Azure file shares without network connectivity to domain controllers. The documented guidance is to choose Microsoft Entra Kerberos when clients lack unimpeded connectivity to AD DS or when storing FSLogix profiles on Azure file shares for Microsoft Entra joined VMs, and the clients must be Microsoft Entra joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined. On-premises AD DS is wrong because it requires clients to be domain joined or to have uninterrupted connectivity to a domain controller. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is wrong because Kerberos authentication requires the client to be domain joined to the Domain Services managed domain; Microsoft Entra joined session hosts do not meet that requirement. Shared Key authorization uses the storage account key and is not identity-based authentication; it cannot enforce per-user permissions.
tags: azure files,microsoft entra kerberos,smb,identity-based authentication,azure virtual desktop

domanda: A service SAS for a blob container references a stored access policy that has the signed identifier reports-read. You must revoke every SAS token bound to that policy while leaving the storage account access keys untouched. Which actions achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Delete the stored access policy named reports-read from the container.
opzione_b: Modify the stored access policy so that its expiry time is a value in the past.
opzione_c: Replace the stored access policy with one that uses a different signed identifier.
opzione_d: Change the container's public access level to Private (no anonymous access).
opzione_e: Add a signedIp (sip) restriction to the SAS tokens that were already distributed.
spiegazione: Deleting the stored access policy revokes the SAS, because Azure Storage can no longer locate the policy named in the signedIdentifier field and denies the request. Changing the expiry time to a value in the past causes any associated signatures to expire. Renaming the policy by changing the signed identifier breaks the association between the existing signatures and the policy, which also revokes them. All three take effect immediately for every SAS bound to the policy, and none of them require regenerating the account keys. Changing the container's public access level is wrong because that setting governs anonymous access only; a SAS is authorized by its signature and keeps working. Adding a signedIp value to tokens that were already distributed is wrong because a SAS token is immutable once signed: altering any field invalidates the signature, and you cannot modify a copy that is already in someone else's hands.

domanda: Which statements correctly describe stored access policies in Azure Storage? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A stored access policy can be defined on a blob container, a file share, a queue, or a table.
opzione_b: A maximum of five stored access policies can be set on a container at one time.
opzione_c: A stored access policy can be associated with an account SAS to enable revocation of that account SAS.
opzione_d: Creating or updating a stored access policy can take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and requests can fail with status code 403 during that interval.
opzione_e: Associating a user delegation SAS with a stored access policy extends the maximum validity of the SAS beyond seven days.
spiegazione: Blob containers, file shares, queues, and tables all support stored access policies. The documented limit is five access policies per container, table, queue, or share at one time; exceeding it returns status code 400 (Bad Request). When you create or update a policy, the change might take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and during that interval requests made with an associated SAS might fail with status code 403 (Forbidden). Option C is wrong: stored access policies are explicitly not supported for an account SAS, which must always be an ad hoc SAS. Option E is wrong for two reasons: stored access policies are not supported for a user delegation SAS either, and a user delegation SAS has a hard maximum expiry interval of seven days that nothing can extend.
tags: stored access policy,limits,account sas,user delegation sas,propagation

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Which statements about identity-based authentication for Azure Files are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: You can use only one identity source for file access authentication per storage account, and it applies to all file shares in that account.
opzione_b: Identity-based authentication is supported for both SMB file shares and NFS file shares.
opzione_c: Share-level permissions are granted by assigning built-in Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor.
opzione_d: Directory-level and file-level permissions are enforced through Windows access control lists (ACLs).
opzione_e: Microsoft Entra Domain Services authentication requires that clients be Microsoft Entra joined.
spiegazione: You can enable only one identity source (on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos) per storage account, and the setting applies to every file share in the account. Share-level access is granted through built-in Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Reader, Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor, and Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor. Granular access below the share is enforced with Windows ACLs on directories and files, just as on a Windows file server. Option B is wrong: Azure Files doesn't currently support identity-based authentication for NFS file shares; the feature applies to SMB shares only. Option E is wrong: for Microsoft Entra Domain Services, Kerberos authentication requires the client to be domain joined to the Domain Services managed domain, not Microsoft Entra joined; being Microsoft Entra joined is a requirement of Microsoft Entra Kerberos instead.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A third-party auditing tool must call Get Blob Service Stats and List Containers against storage account sa1, and it must also read messages from a queue in the same account. Your policy forbids giving the vendor an account key permanently, but the vendor's tool cannot use Microsoft Entra ID. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown to describe the resulting design.
opzione_a: SAS type to issue: [Service SAS | Account SAS | User delegation SAS]
opzione_b: Credential used to sign the token: [Storage account key | User delegation key | Managed identity certificate]
opzione_c: Supported with a stored access policy: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: Fastest way to immediately revoke the issued token: [Delete the stored access policy | Regenerate the storage account key | Call Revoke User Delegation Keys]
risposta_corretta: Account SAS,Storage account key,No,Regenerate the storage account key
spiegazione: Only an account SAS can delegate service-level operations such as Get Service Stats and List Containers and can span more than one service (Blob and Queue) in a single token, so a service SAS is insufficient and a user delegation SAS is ruled out because the tool cannot authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. An account SAS is secured with a storage account key (Shared Key authorization), not with a user delegation key or a certificate. Stored access policies are explicitly not supported for an account SAS, so the token must be an ad hoc SAS: deleting a stored access policy is therefore not an option, and Revoke User Delegation Keys applies only to user delegation SAS. Because there is no policy to delete, regenerating the account key that signed the token is the only way to immediately revoke it.

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: You must generate one account SAS for storage account sa1 that allows a reporting application to enumerate every container in the account, list the blobs inside those containers, and download blob content. The application must not be able to create, overwrite, or delete anything, and it must not reach the Queue, Table, or File endpoints. Select the appropriate value for each SAS query parameter.
spiegazione: SignedServices must be b (Blob) only, because the application must not reach Azure Files, Queue, or Table; bf would add the Azure Files endpoint and bqtf would add all four. SignedResourceTypes must be sco: List Containers is a service-level API and requires the Service (s) resource type, List Blobs is a container-level API and requires Container (c), and Get Blob is an object-level API and requires Object (o). Using o alone or co would omit the resource type needed for List Containers. SignedPermissions must be rl: Read (r) is required for Get Blob and List (l) is required for both List Containers and List Blobs. r alone omits the List permission, and rwl adds Write, which would let the application create and overwrite blobs and containers, violating the requirement. SignedProtocol should be https so that only HTTPS requests are accepted; the default of https,http would also permit HTTP, and HTTP only is never a permitted value for spr.

sotto_argomento: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
domanda: Contoso stores FSLogix profile containers on an SMB Azure file share. The session hosts are Microsoft Entra joined Windows 11 multi-session VMs with no line of sight to the on-premises domain controllers. All users are hybrid identities synced from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Identity source to enable on the storage account: [On-premises AD DS | Microsoft Entra Domain Services | Microsoft Entra Kerberos]
opzione_b: Number of identity sources that can be enabled on the storage account: [One | Two | Unlimited]
opzione_c: Role that grants read, write, and delete access on files and directories at the share level: [Storage File Data SMB Share Reader | Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor | Storage Blob Data Contributor]
opzione_d: Mechanism that enforces directory-level and file-level permissions: [Azure RBAC role assignments | Windows ACLs | Stored access policies]
risposta_corretta: Microsoft Entra Kerberos,One,Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor,Windows ACLs
spiegazione: Microsoft Entra Kerberos is the documented choice when clients lack unimpeded connectivity to AD DS or when storing FSLogix profiles on Azure file shares for Microsoft Entra joined VMs; it requires clients to be Microsoft Entra joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined, which the session hosts are. On-premises AD DS would require connectivity to a domain controller, and Microsoft Entra Domain Services requires the client to be domain joined to the managed domain. You can use only one identity source for file access authentication per storage account, and it applies to all shares in the account; if another source is already enabled you must disable it first. Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor grants read, write, and delete access on files and directories; Storage File Data SMB Share Reader grants read only, and Storage Blob Data Contributor applies to Blob Storage, not to SMB file shares. Below the share, access is enforced with Windows ACLs (also called NTFS permissions) on directories and files; Azure RBAC operates at the share level, and stored access policies relate to service SAS tokens, not to SMB identity-based access.
tags: azure files,microsoft entra kerberos,share-level permissions,windows acls,fslogix,hotspot

domanda: Storage account sa1 contains a blob container named data. A stored access policy named policy1 is defined on data, and several service SAS tokens were issued that reference policy1 through the signedIdentifier (si) field. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) Deleting policy1 immediately revokes every service SAS token that references it. 2) You can specify the expiry time on policy1 and also specify a different expiry time on the SAS token, so that the value on the token overrides the policy. 3) You can associate an account SAS with policy1 so that the account SAS can also be revoked by deleting the policy.
opzione_a: Deleting policy1 immediately revokes every service SAS token that references it.
opzione_b: You can specify the expiry time on policy1 and also specify a different expiry time on the SAS token, so that the value on the token overrides the policy.
opzione_c: You can associate an account SAS with policy1 so that the account SAS can also be revoked by deleting the policy.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: deleting or modifying the stored access policy immediately affects all shared access signatures associated with it, and if Azure Storage can't locate the policy named in the signature, the client can't access the resource. Statement 2 is No: you must specify the start time, expiry time, and permissions either entirely on the SAS token or entirely on the stored access policy; you can't specify the same parameter in both places, and signedExpiry and signedPermissions must be omitted from the URI if they are set in the associated policy. There is no override behaviour. Statement 3 is No: stored access policies are not supported for an account SAS (nor for a user delegation SAS); an account SAS must always be an ad hoc SAS, and the only way to revoke it immediately is to regenerate the account key that signed it.
tags: stored access policy,service sas,account sas,revocation,signed identifier

sotto_argomento: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
domanda: A web API signs in with a managed identity and issues user delegation SAS tokens to its clients so that they can download blobs directly from storage account sa1. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) The API can create the user delegation SAS tokens without ever retrieving a storage account access key. 2) Calling the Revoke User Delegation Keys operation invalidates every user delegation SAS that was signed with the revoked key. 3) If you configure a SAS expiration policy on sa1 with an upper limit of 30 days, a user delegation SAS issued afterwards can be valid for up to 30 days.
opzione_a: The API can create the user delegation SAS tokens without ever retrieving a storage account access key.
opzione_b: Calling the Revoke User Delegation Keys operation invalidates every user delegation SAS that was signed with the revoked key.
opzione_c: If you configure a SAS expiration policy on sa1 with an upper limit of 30 days, a user delegation SAS issued afterwards can be valid for up to 30 days.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: a user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained from Microsoft Entra ID through the Get User Delegation Key operation, so the account key is never needed. The managed identity must simply hold a role that includes the generateUserDelegationKey action, such as Storage Blob Delegator, at the storage account, resource group, or subscription scope. Statement 2 is Yes: when you revoke the user delegation key, any shared access signatures that rely on that key become invalid, and this is documented as the quickest way to revoke a user delegation SAS. Statement 3 is No: a user delegation SAS has a maximum expiry interval of 7 days regardless of the SAS expiration policy, and if the policy is set to a value greater than 7 days it has no effect on a user delegation SAS.
tags: user delegation sas,revoke user delegation keys,sas expiration policy,seven days,managed identity

domanda: Case study: Fabrikam operates storage account fabstor1, which holds a blob container named exports. Three internal applications authorize to fabstor1 by using key1, and they run continuously. An external partner was given a service SAS for exports that references a stored access policy named partner-read; the policy grants Read and List and expires in six months. Fabrikam's security team reports that the partner's SAS URI was leaked in a shared mailbox. You must block the partner's access immediately, and the three internal applications must continue running without any change or outage. What should you do?
opzione_a: Regenerate key1 and key2 on fabstor1.
opzione_b: Delete the stored access policy named partner-read from the exports container.
opzione_c: Configure a SAS expiration policy on fabstor1 with an upper limit of one hour and the Block action.
opzione_d: Set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of fabstor1 to false to disallow Shared Key authorization.
spiegazione: Deleting the stored access policy revokes every SAS bound to it immediately, because Azure Storage can no longer locate the policy named in the signedIdentifier field and denies the request. It affects only the partner's token, so the three internal applications that authorize with key1 are untouched. This is precisely why Microsoft recommends using a stored access policy with a service SAS: it lets you revoke permissions without regenerating the account keys. Regenerating key1 and key2 would revoke the partner's SAS, but it would also cause all three internal applications to fail authorization until they are updated with a new key, which violates the no-outage requirement. A SAS expiration policy only constrains the validity interval of newly created signatures; the Block action denies out-of-policy tokens going forward but is an account-wide control that would also affect signatures the internal applications create, and it is not the targeted revocation mechanism for a policy-bound SAS. Disallowing Shared Key authorization would break the partner's SAS but would simultaneously break all three internal applications that rely on key1. Note that when re-creating a policy later you should use a different signed identifier, because re-creating a policy with exactly the same name would make the leaked SAS valid again.
tags: stored access policy,revocation,service sas,shared key,case study
